problem:
Which of the following are elementary matrices?

Select all that apply.
solution:
An elementary matrix is a matrix obtained from the identity matrix by applying exactly one elementary row operation. 

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

- The matrices $P$ and $Q$ are not elementary matrices because they can't be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying only one elementary row operation.

- The matrix $S$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} &  & {R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =S\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, only $S$ is an elementary matrix.

problem:
Consider the following system of equations.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x-6y-2z &=4 \\ 3x-9y-3z &=6\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
solution:
To classify the system, we first need to find its solution. The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -6 & -2 & 4 \\ 3 & -9 & -3 & 6\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Using the method of Gaussian elimination, we can reduce this matrix to row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -6 & -2 & 4 \\ 3 & -9 & -3 & 6\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & -1 & 2 \\ 3 & -9 & -3 & 6\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x,$ and we have two free variables, $y$ and $z.$ That means we can find $x$ in terms of $y$ and $z.$ 

Therefore, since there are infinitely many solutions, we conclude that the system is *consistent dependent*. 

As a result, only statement “The system is consistent dependent” is true.

Using the formula, we take the alternating sum of the entries in the top row of the matrix, multiplied by their respective minors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(N) & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{7} & 3 & -\frac{1}{7} \\ \frac{1}{7} & 4 & -\frac{1}{7} \\ \frac{1}{7} & 5 & -\frac{1}{7}\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{1}{7}|\begin{aligned}4 & -\frac{1}{7} \\ 5 & -\frac{1}{7}\end{aligned}|-3|\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{7} & -\frac{1}{7} \\ \frac{1}{7} & -\frac{1}{7}\end{aligned}|+(-\frac{1}{7})|\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{7} & 4 \\ \frac{1}{7} & 5\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{1}{7}(-\frac{4}{7}+\frac{5}{7})-3(-\frac{1}{49}+\frac{1}{49})-\frac{1}{7}(\frac{5}{7}-\frac{4}{7}) \\  & =\frac{1}{7}\cdot \frac{1}{7}-3\cdot 0-\frac{1}{7}\cdot \frac{1}{7} \\  & =\frac{1}{49}-\frac{1}{49} \\  & =0\end{aligned}

problem:
Determine the vertical asymptotes of $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}-1}{{x}^{4}-1}.$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator and canceling any common factors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}-1}{{x}^{4}-1} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}-1}{({x}^{2}-1)({x}^{2}+1)} \\  & =\frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{(x-1)(x+1)({x}^{2}+1)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(x-1)(x+1)}}{\cancel{(x-1)(x+1)}({x}^{2}+1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we set the denominator equal to zero:

$$
{x}^{2}+1=0
$$

This equation does not have any real solutions. Therefore, $f(x)$ has no vertical asymptotes.

Let's look at each series in turn.

- For the geometric series $4+3+\frac{9}{4}+\frac{27}{16}+⋯$  the common ratio is

$$

$$

$$

$$

First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{xy}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{zx}-z) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}+0-\frac{1}{z{x}^{2}}-0 \\  & =-\frac{z+y}{{x}^{2}yz} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{xy}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{zx}-z) \\  & =-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}+0-0 \\  & =-\frac{1+x}{x{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{1}{xy}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{zx}-z) \\  & =0+0-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}x}-1 \\  & =-\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(x,y,z)=-\frac{z+y}{{x}^{2}yz}\,i-\frac{1+x}{x{y}^{2}}\,j-\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x}\,k.$ 

Now, we solve $∇f(x,y,z)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{z+y}{{x}^{2}yz}\,i-\frac{1+x}{x{y}^{2}}\,j-\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x}\,k & =0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j+0\text{ }k\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the coefficient of $i$, $j$, and $k$, we obtain:

$$
\begin{cases}-\frac{z+y}{{x}^{2}yz}=0 \\ -\frac{1+x}{x{y}^{2}}=0 \\ -\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x}=0\end{cases}
$$

From the second equation, we get $x=-1.$ Substituting these into the third equation, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x} & =0 \\ -\frac{1+{z}^{2}(-1)}{{z}^{2}(-1)} & =0 \\ 1-{z}^{2} & =0 \\ {z}^{2} & =1 \\ z & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=-1$ into the first equation, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{z+y}{(-1)^{2}yz} & =0 \\ z+y & =0 \\ y & =-z\end{aligned}
$$

When $z=1,$ we have $y=-1$ and when $z=-1,$ we have $y=1.$

Hence, $∇f(x,y,z)=0$ at two points: $(-1,-1,1)$ and $(-1,1,-1).$

$$

In our case, we're given $Q(x,y)=5{y}^{4}{e}^{2x}.$ 

First, let's differentiate $Q(x,y)$ with respect to $x$:

Which of the following sequences diverge?

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
solution:
Let's analyze each sequence in turn. We need to calculate the limit of each sequence as $n$ approaches infinity.

- In sequence “${a}_{n}=\frac{{n}^{3}}{1-{n}^{2}}$ for $n\ge 2$”,  the dominant term in the denominator is $-{n}^{2},$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{{n}^{3}}{1-{n}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{{n}^{3}}{{n}^{2}})}{(\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}-\frac{{n}^{2}}{{n}^{2}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{n}{(\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}-1)} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{n}{0-1} \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

The limit does not exist, so the sequence diverges.

- In sequence “${a}_{n}=\frac{3}{n}$ for $n\ge 1$”, the limit is

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n}={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{3}{n}=0.
$$

The limit exists, so the sequence converges.

- In sequence “${a}_{n}=\frac{2{n}^{2}-3{n}^{3}}{{n}^{3}+5}$ for $n\ge 1$”, the dominant term in the denominator is ${n}^{3},$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{3}$ and get

$$

The limit exists, so the sequence converges.

In conclusion, sequence “${a}_{n}=\frac{{n}^{3}}{1-{n}^{2}}$ for $n\ge 2$” diverges.

problem:
Let $T:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{3}$ be a linear transformation whose standard matrix is $T.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
solution:
Since $T$ is a linear transformation from ${R}^{3}$ into ${R}^{3},$ the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=3 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=3.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement “If $\text{Ker}(T)={[x,y,z]^{T}\,:\,y=z=0}$ then $\text{rank}(T)=2$” is true. Since $y=z=0,$ any vector from $\text{Ker}(T)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=x\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{{v}_{1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $\text{Ker}(T)=\text{Span}{{v}_{1}}.$ Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=1.$ Finally, according the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(T) & =3-\text{nullity}(T) \\  & =3-1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “If $Tx=[1,0,0]^{T}$ has more than one solution, then $\text{nullity}(T)=0$” is false. Since $Tx=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ has more than one solution, there are ${u}_{1},{u}_{2}\in {R}^{3}$ such that  ${u}_{1}\ne {u}_{2}$ and 

$$
T({u}_{1})=T({u}_{2})=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

This means, $T$ is not a bijection and according to the invertible matrix theorem, $\text{nullity}(T)\ne 0.$

- Statement “If $\text{Ker}(T)=\text{Span}{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}$, then $T$ is invertible” is false. Notice that $\text{Ker}(T)=\text{Span}{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}.$ Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=1.$ So, $T$ is not a bijection or, which is the same, $T$ is not invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is “If $\text{Ker}(T)={[x,y,z]^{T}\,:\,y=z=0}$ then $\text{rank}(T)=2$” only.

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
solution:
Since $B$ and $C$ are bases, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ and $C$ are maximally linearly independent sets in ${R}^{2}$ and ${R}^{3},$ respectively, and

- $B$ spans ${R}^{2},$ while $C$ spans ${R}^{3}.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement “${x,{b}_{2},{c}_{1}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$” is false. The set ${x,{b}_{2},{c}_{1}}$ is not a basis of ${R}^{3}$ because the set contains vectors from another vector space.

- Statement “${-2{b}_{3},3{b}_{1},5{b}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$” is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(-2{b}_{3})+{x}_{2}(3{b}_{1})+{x}_{3}(5{b}_{2}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2{x}_{1}){b}_{3}+(3{x}_{2}){b}_{1}+(5{x}_{3}){b}_{2} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{1} &=0 \\ 3{x}_{2} &=0 \\ 5{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} &=0 \\ {x}_{2} &=0 \\ {x}_{3} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Also, ${-2{b}_{3},3{b}_{1},5{b}_{2}}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $B$ can be expressed as a linear combination of ${-2{b}_{3},3{b}_{1},5{b}_{2}}:$

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}(3{b}_{1})+\frac{{x}_{2}}{5}(5{b}_{2})+(-\frac{{x}_{3}}{2})(-2{b}_{3})
$$

- Statement “${{c}_{1},{c}_{2},x}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$” is false. Since $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$, any vector of ${R}^{2},$ including the given vector $x,$ can be written as a linear combination of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ This means that ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2},x}$ is linearly dependent and therefore, cannot be a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is “${-2{b}_{3},3{b}_{1},5{b}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$” only.

problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
solution:
An implication $A⇒B$ is true *unless* $A$ is true and $B$ is false. In other words, the implication is true unless the "promise" is broken.

- Statement “**If** $12$ is divisible by $3$, **then** $9$ is divisible by $4.$” is false. The antecedent "$12$ is divisible by $3$" is true, and the consequent "$9$ is divisible by $4$" is false. So the promise is broken, and the statement is false.

- Statement “**If** $5$ is divisible by $2$, **then** $10$ is divisible by $5.$” is true. The antecedent "$5$ is divisible by $2$" is false, so the promise does not apply. Regardless of the consequent, the promise is *not* broken, and the statement is true.

- Statement “**If** $9$ is divisible by $5$, **then** $6$ is divisible by $3.$” is true. Again, the antecedent "$9$ is divisible by $5$" is false, so the promise does not apply. Regardless of the consequent, the promise is *not* broken, and the statement is true.

Therefore, the correct answer is “**If** $5$ is divisible by $2$, **then** $10$ is divisible by $5.$”; “**If** $9$ is divisible by $5$, **then** $6$ is divisible by $3.$” only.

problem:
Let $p\in Q$ and $q\in Q.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
solution:
First, notice that the statement 

$$
∃\,q,p\in Q,\,p\cdot q=-1
$$

from option $∃\,q,p\in Q,\,p\cdot q=-1.$ reads as follows:

$\,$ There exist rationals $q$ and $p,$ such that $p\cdot q=-1.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement $∃\,p\in Q,\,2p=-1.$ is true, $2p=-1$ for some rational number $p$ (e.g., for $p=-\frac{1}{2}$).

- Statement “The truth set of the predicate $(\,∃\,p\in Q,\,p\cdot q=-1\,)$ is $Q.$” is false. For the predicate

$$
P(q):\,∃\,p\in Q,\,p\cdot q=-1
$$

we note that $P(q)$ is true for some $q\in Q$ and false for others. For example, 

$$
P(0):\,∃\,p\in Q,\,p\cdot 0=-1
$$

is false. However, 

$$
P(1):\,∃\,p\in Q,\,p\cdot 1=-1
$$

is true, since we can take $p=-1.$

- Statement $∃\,q,p\in Q,\,p\cdot q=-1.$ is true. The sentence 

$$
(\,∃\,q,p\in Q,\,p\cdot q=-1\,)
$$

 
can be written as

$$
∃q\in Q\,(\,\underbrace{∃p\in Q,\,p\cdot q=-1}_{P(q)}\,)
$$

which is true whenever the inner predicate $P(q)$ has a nonempty truth set. And according to the discussion in statement “The truth set of the predicate $(\,∃\,p\in Q,\,p\cdot q=-1\,)$ is $Q.$”, this is the case.

Therefore, the correct answer is $∃\,p\in Q,\,2p=-1.$; $∃\,q,p\in Q,\,p\cdot q=-1.$ only.

problem:
Which of the following subspaces must be orthogonal to $\text{Col}(A)$ for every matrix $A?$

Select all that apply.
solution:
Recall that $\text{Col}(A)$ consists of all linear combinations of the columns of $A$, that is, the rows of ${A}^{T}.$

If a vector is orthogonal to every linear combination of the rows of ${A}^{T},$ it must be orthogonal to each row of ${A}^{T}.$
But notice that when pre-multiplying a vector by ${A}^{T},$ we actually multiply each row of ${A}^{T}$ by that vector.
So, $\text{Col}(A)$ must be orthogonal to the left null space of $A,$ which is $\text{Null}({A}^{T}).$

Therefore, the correct answer is $\text{Null}({A}^{T})$ only.

Which of the following are logically equivalent to $R?$

Select all that apply.
solution:
The law that conjunction absorbs disjunction is stated as

$$
R∧(R∨T)≡R.
$$

With that in mind, let's inspect each of the given statements.

- Statement $(T∨R)∧T$ is *not* logically equivalent to $R.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}(T∨R)∧T & ≡T∧(T∨R) \\  & ≡T≢R.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement $R∧(T∨R)$ is logically equivalent to $R.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}R∧(T∨R) & ≡R∧(R∨T) \\  & ≡R.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement $(R∨T)∧R$ is logically equivalent to $R.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}(R∨T)∧R & ≡R∧(R∨T) \\  & ≡R.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $R∧(T∨R)$; $(R∨T)∧R$ only.

problem:
Consider a vector space $V$ and vectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}\in V.$ Given that ${{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ is a linearly independent set and ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},\text{ }{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ is a linearly dependent one, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
solution:
Let's examine each of the given options in turn.

- Statement “${v}_{1}$ is a linear combination of ${v}_{2}$, ${v}_{3}$ and ${v}_{4}$” is true. Since ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ is a linearly dependent set, we obtain that

$$
{x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}+{x}_{4}{v}_{4}=0
$$

has a non-zero solution. Moreover, ${x}_{1}$ can't be zero because then

$$
{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}+{x}_{4}{v}_{4}=0
$$

will have a non-zero solution and that's a contradiction as ${{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ is linearly independent.
Therefore, from ${x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}+{x}_{4}{v}_{4}=0,$ we get

$$
{v}_{1}=-\frac{{x}_{2}}{{x}_{1}}{v}_{2}-\frac{{x}_{3}}{{x}_{1}}{v}_{3}-\frac{{x}_{4}}{{x}_{1}}{v}_{4}.
$$

$$

$$

Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})?$

Select all that apply.
solution:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{(\frac{x}{y})}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}+1}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{(\frac{x}{y})}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}+1}\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement “Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(\sqrt{3},1)$” is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(\sqrt{3},1)$, where we have 

$$
f(\sqrt{3},1)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{1})=\frac{\pi }{3},
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(\sqrt{3},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(\sqrt{3},1) & =\frac{1}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\frac{1}{4} \\ {f}_{y}(\sqrt{3},1) & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “${f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3})$ is defined” is true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(1,\sqrt{3})$, where we have 

$$
f(1,\sqrt{3})=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})=\frac{\pi }{6},
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,\sqrt{3}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is defined” is also true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(0,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,1)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{0}{1})=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(0,1)=-\frac{0}{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is “Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(\sqrt{3},1)$”; “${f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3})$ is defined”; “${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is defined”.

Since $Av=v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =-1$ (but not $1$).

solution:
Recall that the residue classes modulo $n$ have the following properties:

- There are exactly $n$ distinct residue classes modulo $n$

- Two distinct residue classes have an empty intersection: $[a]_{n}\cap [b]_{n}=∅$ if $a≢b\,(\text{mod}\,n)$

- Residue classes modulo $n$ form a partition of the set of all integers: 

$$
Z=[0]_{n}\cup [1]_{n}\cup ⋯\cup [n-1]_{n}
$$

- The integers modulo $n$ is defined as the set containing all distinct residue classes modulo $n$: 

$$
{Z}_{n}=\{[0]_{n},\,[1]_{n},\,…,\,[n-1]_{n}\}
$$

With that in mind, let's now consider each of the given statements.

- Statement “There are $11$ distinct residue classes modulo $11$” is true. There are $11$ distinct residue classes modulo $11.$

- Statement $[7]_{5}\cap [2]_{5}\ne ∅$ is true. Indeed, since $7≡2\,(\text{mod }5),$ we have that $[7]_{5}=[2]_{5}.$ Therefore, $[7]_{5}\cap [2]_{5}\ne ∅.$

- Statement $Z=[0]_{4}\cup [9]_{4}\cup [2]_{4}\cup [15]_{4}$ is true. First, notice the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}[9]_{4} & =[1+4\cdot 2]_{4}=[1]_{4} \\ [15]_{4} & =[3+4\cdot 3]_{4}=[3]_{4}\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[0]_{4}\cup [9]_{4}\cup [2]_{4}\cup [15]_{4} & =[0]_{4}\cup [1]_{4}\cup [2]_{4}\cup [3]_{4} \\  & =Z\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is “There are $11$ distinct residue classes modulo $11$”; $[7]_{5}\cap [2]_{5}\ne ∅$; $Z=[0]_{4}\cup [9]_{4}\cup [2]_{4}\cup [15]_{4}$.

problem:
Which of the following integrals evaluates to zero due to symmetry?

Select all that apply.
solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to zero due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $f(x)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(-x) \\  & =-x(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & \ne -f(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- The function $g(x)={x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-x) & =(-x)^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(-x) \\  & =-{x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(-x) \\  & =-{x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =-g(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-2}^{2}{x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

- The function $h(x)={x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}h(-x) & =(-x)^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡(-x) \\  & ={x}^{2}(-\operatorname{tan}⁡x) \\  & =-{x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\  & =-h(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Hence, the correct answer is ${\int }_{-2}^{2}{x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x$; ${\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x$ only.
